name: Agbekor
summary: An Ewe war dance, once called Atamga, today performed for cultural presentations, in a slow and a fast section. A double bell plays the standard pattern, a rattle plays with and between its strokes, support drums interlock against it, and a lead drum calls the dancers' movements. Ternary time: four main beats of three pulses, with six and three felt against them.

drum_characteristics.feel: Ternary: four dotted-quarter beats of three pulses, the six-feel and the three-feel against them
hallmarks: the bell's standard pattern, the low bell on ONE in the slow section, never stopping
the rattle with the bell and between its strokes, silent on the pulse after ONE
the kagan's 'ups': the second and third pulses of every beat
six against four (3:2) as the basic cross-rhythm
a lead drum calling, a response drum answering

archetype_patterns.name: Agbekor time parts: bell, rattle, kagan
archetype_patterns.function: the parts that do not change for the whole performance

evidence.note: Bell: the standard pattern on pulses 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12 (Locke; Wikipedia, whose example is Atsiagbekor), the low bell on ONE (UVic guide, slow Agbekor). Rattle: 'pa' with the bell, 'ti' between, nothing on pulse 2 (Wikipedia; Locke). Kagan: the ups on the second and third pulses of each beat (Burns, naming Agbekor; Locke, Agbadza). The kidi, totodzi, kloboto and lead drum parts are not given: no Agbekor transcription of them was read.

archetype_patterns.practice_notes: The 'other' lane is the kagan. Count the bell from ONE and from its second stroke: Ewe teachers start it on either.

evidence.note: Tempo: Burns gives 80–120 beats per dotted quarter for Ewe dances at slow to moderate tempo; written here in quarters, 120–180. The fast section is faster; no source read gives its tempo. Open: which support drum carries the six-feel in Agbekor (a 2021 paper says totodzi and kloboto 'carry hemiola patterns' and the kidi 'emphasizes a back beat', read only through a search summary), and the kidi and lead drum themes, which are in Locke's dissertation (1978) and his Worlds of Music chapter, neither read.
